According to recent reports, A total of 11 VUS/CCOP variants (AAC ≥ 10) had absolute effect sizes exceeding 7.99 cm, with P values ranging from 1.6 × 10−4 to 1.1 × 10−31 (five with P < 1.75 × 10−9; Fig. 4 and Supplementary Table 20). Three are NPR2 missense variants classified as VUSs in ClinVar but with large effects on height in our study (between −8.24 and −9.53 cm). Although none of these missense variants achieved genome-wide significance, two (p.G221R and p.R921Q) are experimentally validated loss-of-function variants44. Here we highlight large-effect variants lacking clear clinical annotations (either unannotated or classified as VUSs/CCOPs) that exemplify how population-scale association analyses provide relevant data that clinical geneticists can use to evaluate potentially disease-causing variants.

It has been revealed that we undertook an exome-wide association study in 1,450,633 individuals, identifying 207 height-associated genes after conditioning on common variants—115 more than an earlier large-scale sequencing study9. In 17 genes, singleton pLoFs—the rarest and most deleterious variant class—were associated with absolute effects on height 52× larger than the average common variant (8.92 cm versus 0.17 cm). Although we noted substantial overlap with Mendelian syndromes, fewer than 25% (44 out of 207) of genes include a stature or skeletal growth component in their OMIM description2, and only 16% of height-increasing genes (9 out of 57) are both included in OMIM and annotated with stature or skeletal growth phenotypes. Collectively, rare variant associations indicated strong concordance with genes implicated by common variant associations and reflected established biological processes influencing height, including growth factor signalling, extracellular matrix organization and transcriptional regulation.

In a recent development, our results illustrate classic trade-offs in genetic association studies between effect size and allele frequency. Expanding from singletons to low-frequency variants up to 1%, and from pLoFs to missense variants, increased the number of implicated genes from 17 to 179 but greatly diminished the average absolute effect size. Tests that more explicitly accommodate effect size heterogeneity12 or small proportions of causal variants11 within each gene increased gene discovery another 16%, bringing the total to 207 genes. As no single analysis captured all of the implicated genes, we maximized gene discovery by combining gene-based P values from multiple models using a well-calibrated omnibus gene-based test10.

Industry observers note that the genes we found to be associated with height include those in well-understood pathways but also implicate potentially new areas of height biology. For example, in the GH/IGF pathway, growth hormone (GH1) signals for IGF1 production, stimulating skeletal growth through cartilage generation in the growth plate45. While Mendelian syndromes with altered stature as a major feature are linked to eight members of the GH/IGF pathway—GH1, GHR, GHRHR, GHSR, IGF1, IGF1R, IGFLAS and PAPPA2 (ref. 46)—our results include seven of these eight (Supplementary Table 23), and implicate three others (PAPPA, STC2 and GHRH). Furthermore, for several genes that were previously considered to have autosomal recessive modes of inheritance (GHRHR, IGFALS, IGF1 and PAPPA2), our results show that loss-of-function and deleterious missense variants have apparent effects in the heterozygous state (Supplementary Table 23). Finally, while GH1–IGF1 is generally considered the major driver of post-natal growth and development, the IGF2 pathway is believed to act mainly during prenatal development with uncertain effects on adult height47. Human genetic evidence for a role of the IGF2 pathway in height has previously been limited to extreme short stature (>3 s.d. below average) in Silver–Russell syndrome, caused by disruptions in the IGF2 gene itself (although not implicated here)48. Our results include association in an additional IGF2 pathway gene: IGF2BP2 through singleton pLoFs (β = −8.67 cm, P = 1.52 × 10−10; Table 1), an mRNA-binding protein that stabilizes IGF2 mRNA, providing additional evidence for a developmental role of IGF signalling in adult height.

According to recent reports, accurate complex trait prediction is a key aspiration of human genetics. Current prediction efforts focus on common variants with effects that are individually small but substantial in aggregate. Supplementing this approach by adding both rare variants with individually large effects and burden tests provides substantial predictive value for carriers. Among 337 carriers across our 17 singleton pLoF genes, adding rare variant effects to common variant prediction models improved the prediction performance to nearly that of common variants in the full population (R2 = 0.72 in carriers versus 0.73 across the full sample). However, as these variants are so rare (<0.1% of individuals), this has a limited impact at the population level.

FGFR3 and PTPN11 frequently arose as interesting case studies throughout this work. First, they represent the unusual case in which rare missense variants collectively yielded a significant burden association with no contribution from pLoFs. They reduce height through GoF mechanisms22 and are known causes of achondroplasia7 and Noonan syndrome23, respectively. However, their burden effects were relatively modest (3–15× smaller; −2.31 cm for FGFR3; −4.12 cm for PTPN11) compared with the effects of a few individual variants: −29.8 cm effect for FGFR3 p.G380R; −14.2 cm for PTPN11 p.N308D; and −12.2 cm for PTPN11 p.R265Q. For most other genes, the effect sizes were more consistent for missense and pLoFs and combining them yielded the most statistically powerful analysis.

In a recent development, collectively, this work substantially expands the breadth of rare genetic associations for adult height. Beyond directly implicating 207 genes, we demonstrate how rare variant gene discovery at scale can bridge the gap between common variant GWAS and Mendelian disease genetics, providing valuable data for identifying functional genes and interpreting observed variation in clinical settings.

Our discovery analysis comprised six exome-sequenced cohorts jointly called on an Integrated DNA Technologies (IDT) modified xGen exome capture from the RGC-ME study49: the glaucoma-ascertained African Descent and Glaucoma Evaluation Study III (ADAGES; n = 1,941)50; the Mexico City Prospective Study (MCPS; n = 138,667), comprising residents from the Iztapalapa and Coyoacán districts of Mexico City35; the population-based UK Biobank (UKB; n = 452,583); and three health-system cohorts: Mount Sinai BioMe Biobank (BioMe; n = 26,850), Geisinger Health System DiscovEHR (GHS; n = 165,080)51 and Penn Medicine BioBank (PMBB; n = 40,945)52.

In a recent development, we performed a meta-analysis across six replication cohorts not part of the RGC-ME49. Four cohorts were exome sequenced using a TWIST capture: the household-based prospective ‘BangladEsh Longitudinal Investigation of Emerging Vascular and nonvascular Events’ (BELIEVE; n = 53,830) Study53 and three hospital-based cohorts: The Biobank at Colorado Center for Personalized Medicine (CCPM; n = 48,799)54, Mayo Clinic Project Generation (n = 72,472) and University of California Los Angeles (UCLA) at LA Study (ATLAS) Precision Health Biobank (UCLA ATLAS; n = 38,406). The longitudinal All of Us (AoU) research programme was whole-genome sequenced; participant-level phenotypic and genetic data cannot be removed from the trusted research environment and we therefore did not use AoU data for prediction analyses (AoU; n = 381,888)55. The prospective, population-based Malmö Diet and Cancer Study (MDCS; n = 29,172) was exome sequenced by IDT exome capture but could not be jointly called in the RGC-ME due to regulatory restrictions.

Industry observers note that we calculated an individual’s standing height by first converting all height measurements to centimetres, removing measurements <75 cm or taken before age 18, and then taking the median across the remaining height measurements. We excluded individuals for whom their genetically predicted sex differed from their self-reported sex as well as 76 bone marrow transplant recipients for whom their DNA was collected from blood. Within each cohort, we applied rank inverse normal transformation separately for each sex and used this rank inverse normal transformed height phenotype in genetic association analyses. To approximate height effect sizes in centimetres, we multiplied effect sizes (in s.d. units) by 7.994 cm, the sex-stratified, sample-size-weighted s.d. in the discovery cohorts.

It has been revealed that all genomic data analysed here was generated as previous described9,49,55. In brief, exome capture was performed using IDT (ADAGES III, BioMe, GHS, MCPS, MDCS, PMBB and UKB) or TWIST (BELIEVE, CCPM, Mayo Clinic, UCLA ATLAS) capture reagents, sequencing was performed on the Illumina HiSeq 2500 or NovaSeq 6000 system, and sequencing reads were aligned to GRCh38. AoU used DNA extracted at the Mayo Clinic (blood or saliva) and sequenced at Baylor College of Medicine, Broad Institute, or University of Washington: sequencing centre and DNA source were included as batch covariates55 (Supplementary Fig. 9). PLINK (v.1.9)56 converted the pVCF to PLINK files for downstream analyses. Quality control included sample/variant missingness of <10%, ±10 bp buffer window around target regions, heterozygosity Hardy–Weinberg Equilibrium (HWE) P > 1 × 10−100, excess heterozygosity HWE P > 1 × 10−30 and setting male heterozygous genotypes in the non-pseudoautosomal region (non-PAR) of chromosome X to missing using the PLINK256 option --set-hh-missing. We implemented a previously described support vector machine (SVM)-based quality control protocol to identify likely artefactual variants9 and then used these predictions to create individual-level covariates for GWAS.

Variant Effect Predictor (VEP)57 v.100.4 (Ensembl58 release 100) annotated variants on human protein-coding transcripts and assigned a single consequence per variant based on the canonical transcript defined using MANE58, APPRIS59 and Ensembl canonical tags as previously described58.

We used REGENIE’s60 linear whole-genome regression test to perform three genetic analyses on chromosomes 1–22 and X in the discovery: (1) a TOPMed61 imputed common variant GWAS (AAF > 0.01; n = 19,527,870 variants); (2) a rare variant exome analysis (AAF ≤ 0.01, AAC ≥ 10; n = 9,086,709 variants excluding those tested in the imputed variant GWAS); and (3) a gene-based association analysis of rare coding variation (n = 19,107 gene-level omnibus tests). We set a single unified Bonferroni-adjusted significance threshold of P < 1.75 × 10−9 across all three analyses, accounting for all common, rare and gene-based tests performed (0.05/28,633,686 tests). A discussion of calibration in these results is provided in the Supplementary Note.

It has been revealed that for the non-PARs of chromosome X, we assumed a dosage-compensation model in which homozygous reference male individuals are coded as 0 and hemizygous male individuals are coded as 2 (and heterozygous male individuals were set to missing). In step 1 of REGENIE (that is, prediction of individual trait values based on genetic data), we included genotyped variants with an AAF > 1%, <10% missingness, HWE P > 10−15 and linkage-disequilibrium (LD) pruning (1,000 variant windows, 100 variant sliding windows and an r2 threshold of 0.1). The covariates used in REGENIE steps 1 and 2 are described in Supplementary Table 24.

Industry observers note that to identify conditionally independent common GWAS variants, we performed an iterative conditional meta-analysis using REGENIE’s leave-only-same-chromosome-in (LOSCI) option on TOPMed-imputed dosage data. LOSCI conditions the variant/gene being tested only on the same-chromosome variants to avoid model overfitting. In each iteration, distance-based clumping (1 Mb minimum) identified the lead variant (P < 1.75 × 10−9), which became covariates in subsequent iterations. After 22 iterations, no variants reached significance (P < 1.75 × 10−9), yielding 3,034 independent variants used to condition all rare variant and gene-based association tests (REGENIE’s model includes each variant individually).

REGENIE collapses qualified (based on AAF and annotation) rare coding variants by gene and assigning each individual’s genotype as the maximum of their alternate alleles (2 for individuals who are homozygous alternate carriers for a qualified variant; 1 for heterozygous carriers of any qualified variant; and 0 for individuals who are homozygous reference for all qualifying variants). Burden tests were performed on these genotypes whereby effect sizes represent the per-allele effect of carrying a qualified variant. pLoFs comprised frameshift, stop gain, splice-donor or splice-acceptor variants. Missense variants were evaluated using six in silico predictors: ESM-1v62, SIFT63, PolyPhen2+HumDiv64, PolyPhen2+HumVar64, MutationTaster65 and LRT66. Variants were selected for inclusion in burden tests based on AAF, status as pLoF and—for missense variants—how many algorithms predicted the variant to be deleterious. Missense variants were classified as deleterious if predicted pathogenic by ESM-1v (using a threshold of 0.78) or all five other algorithms; and possibly deleterious if predicted to be not pathogenic by ESM-1v but predicted to be pathogenic by 1–4 other algorithms. Burden tests were then performed using every combination of five different AAF thresholds (singleton (4.17 × 10−7), 0.0001, 0.001, 0.005 and 0.01) and 7 different combinations of variant class: (1) pLoF; (2) pLoF + deleterious missense + stop lost + start lost; (3) pLoF + at least possibly deleterious missense + stop lost + start lost; (4) pLoF + all missense + stop lost + start lost; (5) deleterious missense + stop lost + start lost; (6) at least possibly deleterious missense + stop lost + start lost; and (7) all missense + stop lost + start lost—yielding 35 burden tests.

In a recent development, to properly adjust for multiple correlated tests across a large number of genes, we used gene-P10, an omnibus gene-based test framework that uses ACAT67 to combine P values from four complementary rare variant gene-based tests—BURDEN-ACAT10, Sparse Burden Association Test (SBAT)10, SKAT-O12 and ACAT-V11—into a single P value per gene (Supplementary Fig. 1) as previously described10. After identifying genes associated through gene-P, we quantified the number of significant associations from these four underlying tests (Extended Data Fig. 1a). We classified genes into two groups: burden-associated (P < 1.75 × 10−9 in BURDEN-ACAT or SBAT) or non-burden-associated (P < 1.75 × 10−9 in ACAT-V or SKAT-O and P ≥ 1.75 × 10−9 in both BURDEN-ACAT and SBAT).

We used a previously described method for genetic ancestry assignment49. In brief, using a diverse reference panel comprising 11,354 individuals from 95 populations, we calculated the proportion of haplotype sharing of each sample and assigned them to one of six genetic ancestries (African (AFR), Indigenous American (AMR), East Asian (EAS), European (EUR), Middle Eastern (MEA), and South Asian (SAS)) if they had greater than 50% of that genetic ancestry; those with no majority ancestry were assigned to an ‘OTH’ group. We recognize that these commonly used labels oversimplify an individual’s genetic, cultural and environmental diversity, and use them only out of convenience to properly adjust association tests for genetic ancestry.

In both imputed and sequenced data, we assigned each variant a single AAF representing the maximum AAF across six fine-scale ancestries. On the basis of the fine-scale ancestry maximum AAF, we classified variants as common (AAF ≥ 1%; n = 19,514,636 in imputed data with INFO ≥ 0.3 in all discovery cohorts) or rare (AAF < 1%; n = 44,600,231 in exome data). When a variant was rare (<1%) in the exome, but common in the imputed data (≥1%), we classified them as common (n = 335,522). Singletons in the discovery analysis were defined as those with only a single AAC for variants on chromosomes 1–22 and the X chromosome’s PAR, and a single hemizygous or heterozygous genotype in the X chromosome’s non-PAR. REGENIE used these AAFs and singleton definitions when writing burden test genotypes and running the gene-based tests (options --aaf-file and --set-singleton). For replication analyses, we used the same AAFs as in the discovery analysis but included an additional 12,777,247 unique variants in the replication data. Singletons in the replication comprised variants that were either (1) a singleton in the discovery or (2) a singleton in the replication that was absent from the discovery.

According to recent reports, we compared the pLoF burden effect sizes to common variants identified by GWAS at the same genes by linking conditionally independent GWAS variants to their nearest gene through genomic distance. For genes with multiple nearby GWAS variants, we computed the mean absolute GWAS effect size. For each gene g with kg GWAS loci (where kg > 0), we computed the ratio of the singleton absolute pLoF effect size to the GWAS conditional joint effect size. Specifically, for gene g with singleton pLoF absolute effect size |\({{\beta }}_{g}^{\mathrm{pLoF}}\)| and a set of GWAS conditional joint effect sizes \({\beta }_{1}^{\mathrm{GWAS}}\), \({\beta }_{2}^{\mathrm{GWAS}}\), … , \({\beta }_{{k}_{g}}^{\mathrm{GWAS}}\), we defined the per-gene ratio as:.

These ratios quantify the fold-increase in phenotypic effect conferred by complete gene disruption (through a singleton pLoF carried by an individual) relative to the effect of common regulatory or coding variation at the same locus identified through GWAS. Ratios of >1 indicate that the singleton pLoF has a larger effect on height than the nearby common GWAS variant, consistent with the expectation that rare, gene-disrupting variants tend to have larger per-allele effect sizes than common variants due to stronger purifying selection.

In a recent development, we built a common variant PGS using PLINK56 from 3,039 common (Supplementary Table 8) variants from two sources: first, 3,034 conditionally independent common variants identified through iterative conditional meta-analysis (Methods and Supplementary Table 2) and second, five common variants identified from the exome and not tested with imputed data. The common variant PGS was computed as a weighted sum of alternate alleles, where the magnitude and direction of the weight was based on the estimated variant effect size (in s.d. units) from a joint model in the discovery (n = 826,066; Supplementary Table 1) of all 3,039 variants (Supplementary Table 8) and the same covariates (Supplementary Table 24) used in the association analyses (Supplementary Note).

Sources indicate that we constructed four versions of rare variant PGS (rvPGS), based on the 179 genes with a significant gene-P and either a significant BURDEN-ACAT or SBAT test, weighted using s.d. effect sizes: (1) rvPGSSNP: all 77 significant (P < 1.75 × 10−9, AAC ≥ 10) rare variants in these genes (after LD clumping for variants with R2 < 0.2), weighted by the single-variant effect size; (2) rvPGSpLoF: all 179 pLoF (AAF < 1%, AAC ≥ 10) burden associations weighted by effect size; (3) rvPGSmissense: all 179 deleterious missense (AAF < 1%, AAC ≥ 10) burden associations weighted by effect size; and (4) rvPGSsynonymous: all 179 synonymous (AAF < 1%, AAC ≥ 10) burden associations weighted by effect size. When predicting height based on both rvPGSSNP and burden-based rvPGS, both the burden genotypes and burden effect sizes were recomputed to exclude the variants included in the single-variant rvPGS to enforce independence between the rvPGS.

According to recent reports, all estimations of variance explained by the PGS were performed using genes and effect sizes from the discovery (n = 826,066) but estimated using the replication (n = 242,679 excluding AoU; Supplementary Table 1). First, for each cohort–sex combination (five cohorts × two sexes), a linear regression model was fit of height (in centimetres) on the covariates used in the replication association tests. The PGS of interest was added into the model, and the variance explained was calculated as the difference in adjusted R2 between the two nested models. The reported value was the mean of the ten cohort–sex subsets (five cohorts × two sexes). When computing variance explained by rare-variant PGS, the null model included the 3,039 common variant PGSs (Supplementary Table 8) in addition to covariates (Supplementary Table 24) mentioned above.

In replication cohorts (n = 242,679; excluding AoU; Supplementary Table 1), we predicted an individual’s height (in centimetres) from a mean-centred common variant PGS in s.d. units as follows:.

where \({\bar{\mathrm{height}}}_{\mathrm{cohort},\mathrm{sex}}\) and \({\text{s.d.}}_{\mathrm{cohort},\mathrm{sex}}\) are the mean and s.d. of height among replication individuals matched on cohort and sex.

Although height differs by genetic ancestry, we did not stratify predictions explicitly by genetic ancestry to avoid excluding small subpopulations (Supplementary Table 1). However, most replication cohorts (excluding AoU) comprised individuals of a single genetic ancestry, so stratification by cohort was effectively the same as stratifying by genetic ancestry.

It has been revealed that to predict an individual’s height using rare variants, we calculated various rvPGS using the 179 gene-P genes with significant burden-ACAT or SBAT P value. Owing to the nested nature of burden tests with respect to AAF (for example, a burden test of <1% AAF variants also includes all the variants in a singleton burden test), we restricted to only selecting a specific AAF for each class of variants. We also ensured that in any predictive models including both burden and significant single variants, the burden effects were recomputed without any significant single variants. rvPGS tested include: pLoF AAF < 1%, deleterious missense AAF < 1%, all significant rare variants, height predictions incorporating rare variant PGS (rvPGS) were calculated as:.

To assess the accuracy of any PGS, we report the R2 of a univariate linear model of predicted height on observed height.

The Loss-of-function observed/expected upper bound fraction (LOEUF) metric follows a uniform distribution18 and was available for 201 out of 207 gene-P genes (all but FGD1, HDAC6, IRS4, NRK, SCMH1 and SHOX). We considered genes to be LoF-constrained if they were in the first LOEUF quintile. When comparing whether two gene sets significantly differed with respect to LOEUF, we used a Wilcoxon rank-sum test on LOEUF ranks.

To assess whether height-associated genes identified through rare variant burden testing were enriched for biologically relevant annotations—OMIM disease genes (all and stature/skeletal growth-related, curated in ref. 2), constrained genes and nearest gene to a GWAS signal—we used two-sided Fisher’s exact tests to test for enrichment; when odds ratios were infinite due to zero count cells, we applied a continuity correction of +1 to all cells.

Sources indicate that to address potential confounding by coding sequence (CDS) length, whereby longer genes may be more likely to contain rare qualifying variants and reach significance, we performed a canonical CDS-length-matched enrichment analysis. For each gene, we identified the five closest background genes by canonical CDS length, sampled without replacement, to construct a null set and repeated all analyses described above using these CDS-matched background genes.

Sources indicate that we used a two-sided 2 × 2 Fisher’s exact test to assess whether individuals carrying rare variants were more likely to be observed in the subset of the population based on various thresholds (in s.d. units) of either their predictive error (that is, the absolute difference in the observed and common-variant predicted height; Supplementary Table 18) or their observed height (Supplementary Table 19). The set of genes that we examined included either genes with a significant (P < 1.75 × 10−9) burden test (for example, 17 genes from singleton pLoF burden tests, 8 genes from singleton deleterious burden tests; Fig. 1b and Supplementary Table 6) or all significant gene-P genes with a significant SBAT or burden-ACAT test (Fig. 1d and Supplementary Table 4). While varying the variant class, AAF threshold, gene set and s.d. threshold, we kept the comparison group constant, defaulting to <0.5 s.d. from the mean.

When comparing height association results to ClinVar, height association statistics from the meta-analysis of the discovery and replication cohorts (n = 1.45 million) were used to maximize sample size. For consistency, the list of gene-P genes used for subsetting variants was the list of 207 genes from the discovery only (Supplementary Table 4). ClinVar data were downloaded in July 2025. To subset for diseases with a stature-related component, the union of three filters was used:.

String matching of ClinVar disease column for any of the following strings: stature, height or chondroplasia.

Searching for any of the following manually curated, height-related Human Phenotype Ontology terms in the list of observed phenotype codes: HP:0004322, HP:0003510, HP:0001519, HP:0003498, HP:0003508, HP:0008909, HP:0003502, HP:0008845, HP:0008857, HP:0008848, HP:0011405, HP:0011406, HP:0011404, HP:0011407, HP:0000098, HP:0008873, HP:0003521, HP:0008921, HP:0008922, HP:0008929, HP:0008905, HP:0000002.

It has been revealed that searching the observed phenotype codes for 506 height-related MONDO terms (Supplementary Table 25). This list was generated by MONDO label, definition and synonym fields for the strings stature, height and chondroplasia, and removing any field with the string normal stature.

Any ClinVar entry meeting at least one of these criteria was included in the analysis, yielding 47,763 variants before filtering for those in gene-P genes. While not comprehensive (several variants in Supplementary Table 21 affect known height genes but are not included), this list identifies a set of variants in ClinVar for which the listed diseases are confidently determined to involve stature. Enrichment testing for significant variants in each ClinVar pathogenicity bin (Supplementary Table 22) was performed using the binomial test (probability of success = 1.75 × 10−9).

Tech Report: Newcastle United struggles can be summed up by one word

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Under Eddie Howe, Newcastle United had a clear identity.
  • That was to be a pressing machine, giving teams no time to breathe at times and overrun them in midfield, thanks to physical players such as Tonali and Joelinton.
  • That was the expectation, almost a demand of the Newcastle United fans, as a Wor flags banner read ‘Get into them’.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Under Eddie Howe, Newcastle United had a clear identity.

That was to be a pressing machine, giving teams no time to breathe at times and overrun them in midfield, thanks to physical players such as Tonali and Joelinton.

That was the expectation, almost a demand of the Newcastle United fans, as a Wor flags banner read ‘Get into them’.

Four months on though from Eddie Howe’s departure,  a clear sense of identity is yet to be implemented by Matthias Jaissle.

Jaissle arrived as an unknown to the Premier League, having arrived from Al-Ahli, it has not been smooth sailing so far.

As a club that qualified for the Champions League 18 months ago, is a mid-table finish expected this time around?

It must be stated that this is not the same Newcastle United team that finished top five and qualified for the Champions League in the 2024-25 season.

Having lost the likes of Bruno Guimaraes and Alexander Isak, to Premier League rivals Arsenal and Liverpool respectively. They have lost huge presences in the team and currently lack a talisman to influence a game as well as players such as Isak and Bruno G did multiple times.

Diving deeper, an argument can be made that Newcastle have not hit the same heights since the departure of Alexander Isak in 2025.

Late summer 2025 signings Yoane Wissa and Nick Woltemade struggled for goals, scoring just 14 goals combined between them last season in all competitions. This compares to Isak’s 27 goals in his final Newcastle United season,.

The 2025-26 season saw Newcastle United finish 12th in the Premier League, seven places below where they placed the year before and a massive 17 points worse off.

In a recent development, in my opinion the reasons for this can be summarised into two points, which are lack of away form and dropping points from winning positions. They won just four away games in the Premier League and dropped a crazy 30+ points from winning positions. This suggests Newcastle United have for some time not been the same team that did so well in 2024-25.

Matthias Jaissle officially became Newcastle United Head Coach only 18 days before the start of the season. This gave him little time to bring in players to fit his system of ‘vertical football’ and work his football philosophy into the current players before their first match against Liverpool.

I think it can be said that Newcastle United did start the season well, with three wins and two draws in their first five games (in all competitions).

Industry observers note that after those opening five matches including a Premier League win over Spurs and draws against Liverpool and Bournemouth, I believed that Newcastle would be in a battle for the European places. However, wins have been hard to find. Also a defeat in the Carabao Cup at Everton.

One of the main reasons for the struggles has been the lack of goals from Osula and Wissa, just two between them. Meanwhile out on loan, Nick Woltemade has scored five goals so far for Juventus.

Looking at the wider stats, in the Premier League against Coventry and Everton, Newcastle had 36 shots in total but only eight of those on target, scoring just one goal.

In a recent development, also, new signings have struggled. Fernandez-Pardo without a goal so far, whilst players such as Toure and Bamba are yet to start a Premier League match.

I think Newcastle United’s struggles can at the moment be summed up in one word – change.

Change in manager with new ideas, a change in system still being perfected and big change in the squad with a lot of younger players being brought in who are still adapting to the physicality of the Premier League.

There is though definitely something to build on, the 2-2 draw with Arsenal gave fans hope.

Sources indicate that to answer the question of what the goal for the rest of the season should be, I believe it should be the idea of identity and growth. Allowing Matthias Jaissle to work on his system, find his best team and use this season as a transitional one.

A big challenge will be the big home fixtures against Manchester United and Sunderland, we might know a lot more after these games.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 05:00 EST, 22 November 2026 | Updated: 15:14 EST, 25 November 2026.

In a sport obsessed with the next major thing, there is more attention than ever being paid to teenage prodigies who appear destined for the very top.

In a recent development, the latest player to have fans raving is former Manchester United academy star JJ Gabriel, 16, who joined the club aged nine but stunned those at Old Trafford by asking to leave. He is now closing in on a move to Real Madrid.

The acrimonious nature of the teenager's departure has left Gabriel vulnerable to a spectacular fall from grace, particularly after his team released montages showing him joining an agency and saying goodbye to United.

The spotlight is well and truly burning on Gabriel, and he would do well to learn the lessons of other youngsters who were tipped for greatness but ultimately crashed and burned.

Of course, injuries, personal issues and media pressure can all weigh heavily on a young player's prospects. There are countless pitfalls that mean tomorrow's stars often burn out before they have had the chance to shine.

Here, Daily Mail Sport runs the rule over some of the most famous wonderkids who never managed to live up to their potential.

Wonderkid JJ Gabriel, 16, confirmed his exit from Manchester United on Tuesday night.

In 2004, Freddy Adu was viewed as the future of American football. Dubbed 'The Next Pele', the Ghanaian-born talent was the youngest professional athlete in major American sports when he signed his first contract at just 14.

Recent findings suggest that the hype was extraordinary. He became MLS's highest-paid player, secured a lucrative Nike contract and appeared in an advert alongside Pele himself.

Sources indicate that but things never quite worked out for the attacking midfielder. After three years at DC United and Real Salt Lake, he made the much-anticipated move to Europe, joining Benfica for £1million in 2007. It was largely downhill from there.

Sources indicate that after making just 11 appearances in three years in Portugal, he moved to Monaco before embarking on a series of unsuccessful and increasingly disappointing loan spells in Portugal, Turkey and Greece. He eventually ended up at Brazilian club Bahia in 2013.

From that point, Adu floated around clubs in Brazil, Serbia, Finland, the US and Sweden. He last played competitive fooball for Swedish third-tier side Osterlen in 2021, aged 32. He remains one of football's biggest 'what if' stories.

Freddy Adu was dubbed 'The Next Pele' but he never fulfilled anywhere near his potential.

Once described by Sir Alex Ferguson as 'the best player I have ever seen at his age', Ravel Morrison is a particularly unfortunate case of an English prospect failing to make the most of an extraordinarily promising career.

As a fresh-faced 17-year-old, he arrived at Carrington with the talent and ability to become one of the world's best players.

He had all the attributes of a world-class attacking midfielder and appeared mature beyond his years on the pitch. Off it, however, was a different story.

In early 2011, barely a year after signing his first professional contract with Manchester United, he was charged with witness intimidation in connection with a domestic violence case.

It has been revealed that since then, although he has never served time in prison, Morrison has faced several further charges, including assault, harassment and fraud. His repeated off-field troubles ultimately derailed a career that had once promised so much.

Recent findings suggest that morrison has gone on to represent 15 clubs during a career spanning 16 years, failing to fulfil the promise that once enchanted Ferguson. He is at the moment plying his trade in the second tier of UAE football.

Ravel Morrison was one of the most talented players to come through Man United's academy.

The first Brazilian on this list is former Manchester City forward Robinho. Having come through the Santos academy – a production line that has also delivered the likes of Pele and Neymar – he was expected to become the next superstar to emerge from the club's illustrious ranks.

However, a series of setbacks meant he never quite fulfilled that early promise. Robinho followed in the footsteps of Brazilian stars such as Adriano, Dani Alves and Kaka by moving to Europe at a young age, joining Real Madrid in 2005.

He enjoyed a promising start to his career, making more than 100 appearances for Los Blancos and winning two league titles before turning 24.

In a recent development, but his move to Manchester City in 2008 failed to take his career to the next level. In fact, things began to unravel.

Industry observers note that the Brazilian did not get off to the best of starts. Upon arriving in Manchester, he revealed that 'Chelsea had made a great proposal, and I accepted'.

What followed were two underwhelming years at the Etihad, where he scored 16 goals in 53 appearances and spent much of his second season in England sidelined by injury.

Recent findings suggest that robinho subsequently joined AC Milan before spells with a number of Turkish clubs and a return to Brazil. He never again reached the heights of his early career.

In a recent development, the Brazilian is currently imprisoned after being found guilty of sexual assault in connection with an incident at a Milan nightclub in 2013. He began serving his nine-year sentence in 2024.

Former Man City star Robinho never quite fulfilled the early promise he had back in Brazil.

Another case reminiscent of Adu's: a young superstar who was seemingly rated too highly before we ever really got to see him play.

In a recent development, mastour caught the eye of Italian giants AC Milan after gaining notoriety on YouTube. His video, uploaded in 2012 and titled 'The Best 14-year-old in the World', showcased the Moroccan's impressive array of skills and tricks, making him one of football's first viral sensations.

Recent findings suggest that the hype surrounding Mastour was staggering, with the youngster securing a lucrative endorsement deal with Nike. Before long, he was posing alongside Neymar in a photoshoot.

But the success never materialised for the tricky forward. During four years on AC Milan's books, he failed to make a single first-team appearance and managed just six outings during loan spells at Malaga and Dutch side PEC Zwolle.

The Moroccan, now 28, plays in the fourth tier of Italian football. Quite how such a highly rated prospect failed to fulfil his potential remains a mystery.

Hachim Mastour dazzled as a teenager on the internet but ended up a long way from the top.

From one player who never highlighted his quality to one who only a decade ago was the recipient of the coveted Golden Boy award for the best under-21 player in Europe.

Renato Sanches was an absolute phenomenon, the box-to-box midfielder burst onto the scene in the 2015-16 season at Benfica – earning himself a place on the plane to France with Portugal for the 2016 Euros where he played a pivotal role in his nation's triumph.

Those performances saw a host of European giants fight it out to land the then-18-year-old, with Bayern Munich emerging triumphant – landing the midfielder in a deal rising to £63million.

However, Sanches failed to hit his stride in Germany and he was soon shipped out on loan to Swansea – where he was best remembered for passing the ball to an advertising hoarding.

Recent findings suggest that he enjoyed a small resurgence at Lille, winning Ligue 1 and the French Super Cup, paving the way for a move to PSG. But once again, the significant transfer failed to work out, and he now finds himself with Greek side Panathinaikos.

He enjoyed a resurgence at Lille, winning Ligue 1 and the French Super Cup, which paved the way for a move to Paris Saint-Germain.

But once again, a massive-money move failed to work out, and he now finds himself at Greek side Panathinaikos.

Renato Sanches (pictured at Roma in 2024) now plies his trade in Greece with Panathinaikos.

Alexandre Pato had the world at his feet, but his body ultimately failed to deliver on the extraordinary talent he possessed.

Industry observers note that the Brazilian was an electric centre-forward who lit up European football. His goal against Barcelona in the Champions League, scored after just 24 seconds at the age of 22, was a perfect illustration of his frightening ability.

His pace, agility and clinical finishing saw him touted as a future world-beater, while he was named Golden Boy.

Alexandre Pato is another wonderkid who saw their career hampered by a string of injuries.

Yet persistent injury problems made it almost impossible for Pato to fulfil his early promise.

Recent findings suggest that the Brazilian struggled with ankle, Achilles and muscle problems throughout his career. As the injuries mounted, his outstanding physical attributes began to wane, rendering the qualities that had once terrified defenders increasingly ineffective.

After six years at AC Milan, Pato returned to Brazil to join Corinthians. He spent two years with the club before embarking on short spells at Chelsea and Villarreal, neither of which yielded lasting success.

Rounding off this list is another English talent who once looked destined for the very top but has since seen his career take a downward turn.

Industry observers note that back in 2019, there were few hotter prospects in world football than Jadon Sancho. The then 19-year-old had made the brave decision two years earlier to leave England, having spent several impressive years in Manchester City's academy, and join Bundesliga giants Borussia Dortmund.

It seemed a bizarre move at the time, but the switch proved to be a stroke of genius. Sancho was handed regular first-team football and flourished, registering 40 goals and 54 assists in just 118 Bundesliga appearances. He also collected a DFB-Pokal winner's medal.

By 2021, the boy from Kennington had the world at his feet, with a host of suitors willing to break the bank to secure his services.

Jadon Sancho once had the world at his feet but has found himself stuck in a downward spiral.

After a summer-long transfer saga, Sancho eventually joined Manchester United for an eye-watering £73million, reportedly earning £350,000 per week. It proved to be a nightmare move for both parties.

The Englishman had to wait until late November to score his first United goal in his debut season and never consistently rediscovered his best form.

In January 2024, he returned to Germany and enjoyed a revival, helping guide Dortmund to the Champions League final, where they lost to Real Madrid at Wembley.

It has been revealed that two unsuccessful loan spells at Chelsea and Aston Villa followed before Sancho left United as a free agent last summer. He remains without a club at the age of 26, just five years after his mega-money move.

For all the promising youngsters who struggle to live up to the hype, there are also teen sensations who navigate the pitfalls of professional football to achieve great things.

It has been revealed that kylian Mbappe helped Monaco win their first Ligue 1 title for 17 years having broken into the team as a 16-year-old. His progress since then has been remarkable and he remains one of the world's very best at Real Madrid.

His team-mate Vinicius Jr signed for Real Madrid to much fanfare as an 18-year-old and has lived up to it all for both club and country.

While you could argue that Neymar could have achieved more, he has still enjoyed a stellar career across the globe and become the highest-scoring Brazilian player in history for the national side after signing for Barcelona, as one of the most talked-about starlets.

Wayne Rooney broke through for Everton at 16 and went on to have a brilliant career.

When you look closer to home, Wayne Rooney and Michael Owen broke through as exciting 16-year-olds and both reached the very highest level.

Paolo Maldini made his AC Milan debut at 16 and became one of the all-time great centre-backs and Cesc Fabregas developed into a world class midfielder after getting selected at the same age for Arsenal.

Going back further, Diego Maradona was playing senior football at 15, as did Ronaldo Nazario, while Lionel Messi embarked on his extraordinary career at 16.

JJ Gabriel and his management will be hoping that when all is stated and done - his name is associated with this category and avoid joining the starlets who never quite made it.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Joel Lefevre | 25 Nov 2026 14:16, Last updated: 25 Nov 2026 14:19.

On Friday, the Columbus Crew can pull off what may become the biggest upset in MLS playoff history and eliminate Inter Miami in game two of that first-round series at ScottsMiracle-Gro Field.

Last weekend the Crew took game one by a 3-0 score, putting them in position to eliminate the reigning champions should they win this upcoming fixture.

Columbus had a lot of momentum heading into the playoffs, and that continued on Saturday as they took advantage of some sloppy Miami defending to take a surprising lead in this series.

Laurent Courtois has seen his side score three or more goals in four of their last five matches versus MLS opposition, while posting a clean sheet in three of those instances, making them an appealing option to choose on the UK betting sites.

The Crew exposed gaps in the Miami squad, scoring on three of their five targeted efforts last weekend and putting the Herons on the ropes heading into game two.

This is only the second time they are up 1-0 since this best-of-three first-round format was introduced, with this team advancing past Atlanta United in three games on the only previous occasion in which they were in this position in 2023.

Only once since their 2015 MLS Cup final defeat versus the Portland Timbers have they lost a post-season match at home, with the New York Red Bulls blanking them 1-0 in game one of that opening round series in 2024.

Friday will mark the second time the Crew can eliminate Miami from a major competition in Columbus, after knocking them out of the 2024 Leagues Cup thanks to a 3-2 victory at ScottsMiracle-Gro Field in the round of 16.

For a team boasting so much experience and talent in the biggest club and international competitions, Inter Miami failed to keep their composure in numerous instances last weekend.

Saturday’s defeat was the joint-worst for the club in the post-season, though given everything that transpired, they could be looking much worse heading into this match.

Kily Gonzalez will be relieved to know that Lionel Messi is available, escaping with just a caution in game one after throwing the ball at Gonzalo Tapia, a moment some believed should have warranted a sending off for the Argentine.

Miami played a good portion of that match a man down, and have never won the second game in a best-of-three MLS playoff series.

The Herons have given up a combined six goals in their last two matches versus MLS opposition and have yet to beat an MLS club in a knockout fixture this season.

The reigning league champions have lost four of their five all-time playoff outings away from home, with their only triumph coming at FC Cincinnati in 2025 (4-0).

Columbus Crew Major League Soccer form:.

Columbus Crew form (all competitions):.

Inter Miami Major League Soccer form:.

Due to a cruciate ligament tear, Wessam Abou Ali will not be available for Columbus in game two of this series.

Gonzalo Tapia netted twice in Miami, with Taha Habroune also scoring as Patrick Schulte made three stops for the clean sheet.

On the Miami side, Mateo Silvetti is dealing with a shoulder matter, Tadeo Allende still has a knee problem and Israel Boatwright is recovering from a cruciate ligament tear.

Gonzalo Lujan will be suspended following his red card in game one, while Sergio Reguilon, David Ayala and Cesar Abadia are all questionable with lower-body injuries.

Columbus Crew possible starting lineup:.

Schulte; Farsi, Moreira, Zawadzki, Amundsen; Zaroury, Chambost, Habroune, Rodriguez, Tapia, Mendez.

Inter Miami possible starting lineup:.

In a recent development, st. Clair; Fray, Casemiro, Micael, Falcon; De Paul, Bright, Segovia; Messi, Suarez, Berterame.

While Miami have all they need to come back and win this series, they are far too rigid defensively and give away too many quality scoring opportunities, which is why we believe their season will end much earlier than most would have expected.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In your opinion, what are the key problems that Newcastle United face?
  • Not the greatest start to the season, so where has it all gone wrong compared to qualifying for the Champions League and winning the Carabao Cup in 2025?
  • After a poor 2025-26 season and the departures of Bruno Guimarães, Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali, the club needed to bring in proven replacements.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In your opinion, what are the key problems that Newcastle United face?

Not the greatest start to the season, so where has it all gone wrong compared to qualifying for the Champions League and winning the Carabao Cup in 2025?

After a poor 2025-26 season and the departures of Bruno Guimarães, Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali, the club needed to bring in proven replacements.

Instead, Newcastle United have signed young, unproven players. Bazoumana Touré, Aladji Bamba and others are not ready to replace players like Gordon and Tonali. There is also no guarantee that they will ever reach that level.

The summer recruitment simply wasn’t good enough.

Most Newcastle United fans still support Matthias Jaissle but there are concerns about the way the team is playing.

Some have criticised Jaissle’s tactics, he uses the Red Bull philosophy which is built around intense pressing, quick transitions, vertical attacks and athletic players. While this style can be effective, it is not always easy to get right.

Sources indicate that newcastle Unite need to find a way to make these tactics work with the players they have. In my opinion the performances have not been good enough, questions are starting to be asked.

Another major problem is the lack of experience in the Newcastle United squad, young players need time to develop.

When you are trying to compete in the Premier League you need experienced players in the here and now who can handle pressure and help the team through difficult periods.

Losing experienced players has left a big gap in the squad and Newcastle United need players who can make an immediate impact, not just players who might become good in a few years.

In my opinion, Newcastle United seem to have lost some of the identity that made them successful. The team used to play with energy, intensity and passion, difficult to play against.

Performances have become inconsistent, supporters need to see a team that fights for every ball and gives everything for the badge.

Newcastle United need to get their recruitment right, the club cannot overly rely on young players who are not ready to make an immediate difference.

They also need to find consistency under the manager. The tactics need to suit the players, the team needs to show the same energy and desire that made them successful in the past.

There is still time for Newcastle United to turn things around but changes need to happen soon.

By Matt Law | 25 Nov 2026 14:30, Last updated: 25 Nov 2026 14:32.

Manchester United are expected to be active during the January transfer window, with the club potentially making three mid-season signings.

The Red Devils currently find themselves down in 19th spot in the Premier League table and facing what would be a stunning relegation from the top flight.

There could also be first-team departures in the winter market, as newly introduced head coach Mauricio Pochettino begins to shape the squad.

Here, Sports Mole looks at five players who could potentially leave Old Trafford when the January market opens for business.

Zirkzee was linked with a move away from Man United over the summer, but he was ultimately not allowed to depart due to the fact that the Red Devils were unable to sign a replacement.

Even with Benjamin Sesko out injured, Zirkzee has not started a single match this season, with each of his 11 appearances coming off the bench.

The Netherlands international has scored twice this season, but his overall record for Man United since arriving from Bologna in 2024 is 11 goals in 86 appearances.

It has been a struggle for the 25-year-old in English football, but he is not short of interest, and a return to Serie A in January is seen as a serious possibility at this stage.

Como and Napoli are the latest clubs to be linked with Zirkzee.

Mazraoui is reportedly attracting the attention of AC Milan ahead of the January market, with a mid-season departure for the Morocco international thought to be possible.

The 29-year-old has underperformed in his nine appearances for Man United this season and is not believed to be in the club's long-term plans.

Initially, the defender impressed after arriving from Bayern Munich, and he has now represented the Red Devils on 86 occasions in all competitions.

However, a switch in the January market could be on the cards, especially if Man United are able to boost their options at full-back in the winter window.

Heaven is reportedly open to the idea of leaving Man United during the winter market.

The 20-year-old has made eight appearances for the Red Devils this season, including five outings in the Premier League, but he was an unused substitute against Liverpool in the team's last match, which ended in a 4-0 defeat.

Man United are expected to bring in a new centre-back in January, and Heaven is mentioned to be concerned over what that would mean for his playing time.

As a result, the Englishman is allegedly open to a winter loan move, while a permanent exit is not being ruled out depending on what offers arrive.

Heaven, who has a contract with Man United until the summer of 2029, has made 32 appearances for the club since arriving from Arsenal in February 2025.

Martinez's contract with Man United is due to expire at the end of the campaign, and there is no getting away from the fact that it has been a tough season for the Argentine.

A latest deal for the 28-year-old is seen as highly unlikely given that he has openly criticised Man United chiefs, such as director of football Jason Wilcox, during the 2026-27 season.

Man United will be reluctant to lose the Argentina international on a free transfer, so it is possible that a sale in the January window could occur, depending on the offer.

Martinez has been one of the team's biggest under-performers this season, and it appears that his time at Old Trafford will come to an end at some stage in 2027.

Amass may yet be given the chance to prove himself to fresh Man United head coach Pochettino, but the defender's future looks to be away from Old Trafford.

The 19-year-old was heavily linked with a departure during the summer window, but he stayed at Man United past the deadline and has made two appearances this season, both in the Champions League.

Amass was not in the squad against Liverpool last time out, though, and Luke Shaw's return to fitness has pushed him further down the pecking order.

A number of Championship clubs are believed to be keen on the teenager, who only has a deal with the 20-time English champions until the end of the season.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Watching last night’s woeful performance against Portsmouth unfold, I was struck by the similarity in playing style of one current West Ham winger with a previous playing enigma from whom West Ham could never seem to coax the best.

Triggered by the  irritation generated from watching Manor Solomon constantly check back, slow down play and then inevitably cut inside, I found myself comparing him with another West Ham winger who repeated the same trick ad nauseam.

Even on the one occasion when he was put clean through beyond his full back, by a brilliant pass from Ezra Mayers, Solomon got to the by line and – infuriatingly, checked back instead of trying to cross with his weaker foot.

And at that moment I thought “Saïd Benrahma” all over again.

The enigma that was Saîd Benrahma: at least he scored a few, created a few, and smacked a mean penalty past Fiorentina’s keeper in the summer of 2023.

‘Benny’ could at least create chances (and score a mean penalty) whereas Manor Solomon just runs down blind alleys, head down, inevitably slowing and cutting inside to use his right foot.

Sources indicate that exactly as, on numerous occasions in each game, the Algerian would check back, infuriatingly, and slow up play instead of pressing on to beat his full back on the inside or out. In that respect Solomon seems identical, disrupting West Ham’s flow, allowing defenders to reset and frustrating the bejesus out of supporters.

At least Benrahma could create and occasionally score: Solomon has, by the reckoning of westhamworld.co.uk, now played “1141 minutes for two goals and two assists, averaging a goal every 285 minutes”.

For whatever reason the Israeli clearly is a shadow of the player who helped fire Leeds to promotion and West Ham need to consign him to the same ‘rest and recuperation’ home in which Mads Hermansen has been sent to recapture his form.

Austbo at least has a shot on him and seems to be able to beat players inside and out: With the Norwegian there is the feeling that there’s more to come. With Solomon, exactly as Tottenham fans suggested, the fear is that his best days are long in the rear view mirror. Much like Saîd Benrahma, but without the trophy to show for it.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that diet Pep is losing his fizz.
  • Seven successive Premier League wins to start his City reign, a record for a new manager in the competition, breaking one jointly-held by Guardiola, gave the impression that this might be a smooth passing of the torch after all.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 07:00 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 05:23 EST, 26 November 2026.

Sources indicate that diet Pep is losing his fizz. Enzo Maresca may look like Pep Guardiola, may have learned his craft under his Manchester City predecessor, but his quest to follow in his mentor’s footsteps has all gone a bit flat.

Seven successive Premier League wins to start his City reign, a record for a new manager in the competition, breaking one jointly-held by Guardiola, gave the impression that this might be a smooth passing of the torch after all.

Three months in, and three defeats on the spin that left them six points behind Arsenal have made it clear that something is not clicking for Maresca.

Is the uncertainty around the potential punishment following that guilty verdict taking its toll? Is Maresca just suffering from his usual late autumn dips? He suffered similar tricky periods around late October and early November at Leicester and his first season at Chelsea too.

Or is there something at the heart of his side, of his system, that’s finally being exposed?

Enzo Maresca's Man City have slumped to three straight Premier League defeats after a promising start to the season.

Sources indicate that guardiola’s City was all about control. Keep the ball, dominate the pitch, play the game at your pace, on your terms.

Sources indicate that maresca’s City, regardless of how well they started the season, has been about anything but. It has been about triumph amid chaos, about moments of magic more than the overarching method.

According to recent reports, without that control, City’s defensive issues have been laid bare. The 13 goals they have let in after 10 games is their most at this stage since 2008. They haven’t kept a clean sheet in their last eight matches in all competitions. That's a drought longer than at any point under Guardiola.

Their biggest problem over City's three successive Premier League defeats is just how susceptible they have been to counter attacks.

Only Newcastle have faced more shots this season following ‘fast breaks’ – data giants Opta's term for counter attacks – than City’s 17, and 11 of those have come in the last three games: six against Nottingham Forest, two of which led to goals, three against Brighton and another two against Aston Villa.

In a recent development, maresca’s side are being more profligate in possession, too. Over the first seven games of the season, they lost the ball 120 times a game on average – one of the best figures in the division. Since then, it’s closer to 140.

City have been wasteful in possession and regularly overrun on the counter, with Elliot Anderson (centre) too often left isolated in midfield.

ANDERSON CAN'T DO IT ALL ON HIS OWN.

Sources indicate that many of these problems have their roots in Maresca's serious problems in midfield. Rodri, the best holding midfielder of his generation, was always going to be hard to replace but Maresca appears to be expecting Elliot Anderson to do it all on his own.

Sources indicate that anderson is at his best when he’s free to get up and down the pitch, box to box, using his physicality not just in winning the ball back but progressing it. No midfielder played more passes into the final third last season than Anderson at Forest. At one stage of the campaign, he had played more progressive passes than any other player across Europe’s top five leagues.

And yet Maresca is forcing Anderson to play as the sitter while his golden boy Enzo Fernandez, whom he pushed City to sign in the summer for £125million, is roaming free and high up the pitch.

Maresca likes his teams to build up in a 3-1-6 shape, which sees Fernandez push up as an extra attacking midfielder, and leaves Anderson manning the fort alone.

When City lose the ball, though, it leaves them wide open.

This is the opening goal City conceded against Forest. Josko Gvardiol wants to play the ball inside but has only red shirts and empty green space ahead of him. Anderson is the only man free, but even he is too high and has a Forest player ready to cut off the pass. Eventually, Gvardiol gets robbed and Forest score.

Recent findings suggest that A lack of options for Josko Gvardiol (left) led to Forest's opener against City. Enzo Fernandez (circled) was caught high up the pitch, way ahead of the deeper Anderson (also circled).

Here’s another moment in the defeat by Brighton.

The Seagulls break forward on the flank and Anderson races over to close the ball down. Fernandez is, you guessed it, high up the pitch.

City have no midfield cover to stop the ball inside, Abdukodir Khusanov gets drawn in and leaves loads of space in behind for Yasin Ayari to exploit and cross to Maxim De Cuyper for a great chance.

The lack of protection offered by Anderson and especially the more advanced Fernandez was again on show against Brighton, who were able to exploit the acres of space left in midfield.

Sources indicate that fernandez is doing what Maresca wants, but it’s not working. Maresca needs more from him, especially when Anderson’s instincts are to press and harass and bully, which can leave gaps when he does not yet read the game as comprehensively as Rodri.

It has been revealed that anderson sits in the top five for ball recoveries among midfielders to have played 500 minutes this season. Fernandez is in the bottom five. That figure becomes even more alarming when you consider Anderson has created more chances from open play than Fernandez, too.

Ayyoub Bouaddi demonstrated at the World Cup that he had the most similar profile to Rodri. It might be time for Maresca to put some faith in him.

It has been revealed that maresca has always wanted his goalkeeper to be an 11th outfielder. In his one season at Leicester, Mads Hermansen played more passes than any goalkeeper in Championship history. During his time at Chelsea, there was a shaky moment in a draw with Arsenal when loud groans greeted a misplaced pass from Robert Sanchez.

‘I am the guy who asks Robert to do that,’ said Maresca after that game. ‘The moment he stops doing that, he is not going to play.’.

According to recent reports, donnarumma, though, for all his (usually) excellent shot-stopping, is anything but a ball-playing goalkeeper. The ball rolled under his foot from a simple back pass against Coventry and so nearly crept over the line. He gifted France an early lead while on international duty with Italy when he passed the ball straight to Michael Olise.

Only two keepers made more errors leading to shots than Donnarumma across the course of last season, with many of those being with his feet, like when he gifted Kai Havertz an equaliser in City's victory over Arsenal in April.

Gianluigi Donnarumma has never been good with his feet - now his excellent shot-stopping has taken a dip too.

The Italian should have easily dealt with Nicolas Jackson's second goal in City's 2-1 loss at Aston Villa.

The decision to let James Trafford leave in the summer, especially with Guardiola’s impending departure and a manager like Maresca coming in, is looking ever more misguided.

Trafford is not immune to mistakes either, of course. He erred badly when trying to play out from the back for City against Spurs last season and made an almost identical howler for Leeds at Bournemouth in October. But he is still far more confident at playing out from the back than Donnarumma.

The double blow for Maresca is that the trade-off with Donnarumma – where he makes up for his weakness with the ball at his feet by making saves that other keepers can’t make – is no longer paying off either.

Nicolas Jackson’s shot squirmed straight through him to hand Villa victory and condemn City to their first defeat of the season.

When you are coughing up chances as frequently as City are, Maresca needs his keeper to be on top form.

It has been revealed that do you know who is keeping the ball out of his net? James Trafford. He boasts the highest save percentage of any goalkeeper in the top flight, keeping out 81 per cent of the shots on target coming his way. Donnarumma is 15th, on less than 66 per cent.

Recent findings suggest that according to Opta’s expected data, Trafford has also prevented more than four goals that he should have conceded from the quality of the shots he’s faced. Again, he’s the best in the Premier League. Donnarumma is middle of the pack.

‘At the moment, I’m not thinking about the goalkeeping situation,’ said Maresca recently. Without Trafford there and just 34-year-old Geronimo Rulli as back-up, he doesn’t really have a choice but to persist with Donnarumma and hope he improves.

When the goals stop flowing for Erling Haaland, City can't mask all their other problems.

So used are we now to seeing the Norwegian on the scoresheet, having notched nine in City’s opening eight matches, that when he goes just two games without a goal it feels as if he’s on a barren spell.

The issue, though, is less down to Haaland and more that City’s build-up in recent weeks is struggling to get him into the game.

Recent findings suggest that city are finding it more difficult to get Haaland on the ball. His touches per game are falling steadily but, crucially, so are the quality of the chances his team-mates are creating for him.

Haaland had more than one Opta-defined 'big chance' in five of City’s opening seven games. He’s had just one come his way in each of their three defeats.

His expected goals (xG) tally is dropping too. Across City’s winning streak, Haaland’s average xG per match was 0.81. Only once, against Liverpool, did it drop below 0.5.

Over the three defeats, it’s just 0.45 and has not once gone above 0.5.

Antoine Semenyo missing the last three games through injury has not helped, especially when teams now try to pack the middle of the pitch and force City wide.

Haaland will come good, he always does, but City need to start serving him again if Maresca wants to get through this tricky spell and stop the vultures from circling.

Sure it couldn’t happen, could it? Only five times in the history of the Premier League have sides suffered successive relegations from the top tier to the third.

For anyone who witnessed the shambolic showing at Fratton Park on Tuesday night, that nightmare scenario suddenly doesn’t look so  ridiculous. West Ham in the third division, 62,500 seater stadium and all?

Alarming parallels exist between West Ham’s performance this season and that of their former competitors Leicester City who now find themselves playing their football in the third division.

Industry observers note that the Hammers are now in the bottom half of the Championship, with just 24 points from 17 games. At the same stage last season, the Foxes themselves, after 17 games had amassed … Exactly the same number of points.

All of which seemed unimaginable when the Irons beat Swansea five weeks ago to go second, and Nuno Espirito Santo picked upthe September manager of the month award.

According to recent reports, fratton Park showing was a real wake up call to West Ham’s management and board. This ship is sinking.

The only positive is that a month is a long time in this league. A run of form could be just around the corner and any team – West Ham included – can win five or six games and transform their fortunes. But the Hammers’ form at present is most definitely that of a relegation candidate rather than a play-off hopeful.

Which hardly helps the recruitment in January.

For anyone living under the misconception that Leicester City’s case was an isolated example and that lightning couldn’t strike twice, Wolverhampton Wanderers, who were also relegated in 2012/13, had 22 points after 17 games.

According to recent reports, stoke City come calling on Saturday with a seriously impressive run of form, unbeaten in six whereas the Hammers are winless in their last half dozen. No time like the present to get back to winning ways and arrest the downhill slide. One relegation is enough, thank you very much.

  • The reigning MLS Cup runners-up captured game one 2-0 last Sunday, putting them one win away from round two in the Western Conference playoffs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Joel Lefevre | 25 Nov 2026 14:36.

Real Salt Lake will try to extend their season into next week with a Friday win over the Vancouver Whitecaps at America First Field in game two of that best-of-three playoff series.

The reigning MLS Cup runners-up captured game one 2-0 last Sunday, putting them one win away from round two in the Western Conference playoffs.

After surviving a nervy shootout in the Wild Card Round, Salt Lake are now on the brink of elimination yet again after a subpar showing in game one against the Caps.

On Sunday, Pablo Mastroeni’s men suffered just their second defeat in their last eight MLS outings and were second-best for much of the game.

While they are on the verge of another early exit, they can draw optimism from being unbeaten in their last four MLS affairs at America First Field.

During the regular season, Salt Lake showed strong attacking potency on home soil, netting three or more goals six times and scoring multiple times on 12 separate occasions.

They will try to end a five-match playoff losing run on Friday, scoring a goal or fewer in each of those instances.

Claret and Cobalt have not lost a playoff match at home in 90 minutes this decade, with their only such victory at America First Field occurring on penalties versus the Houston Dynamo in game two of that opening round series.

It is just one game, but Vancouver looked very much like title contenders as they began the 2026 MLS post-season in style.

Jesper Sorensen’s side carried the play throughout game one and will seek a fifth consecutive MLS triumph on Friday.

While this is the fourth straight year the Caps are in the post-season, they have won only once in that span in normal time away from home, beating San Diego 3-1 in the Western Conference Final last year.

Meanwhile, they failed to win three of their final four regular-season away fixtures this season against Western Conference opposition, with the highest-scoring team in the West failing to score on two of those occasions.

Vancouver have never lost a playoff encounter under Sorensen when netting first but have also never won a post-season outing in 90 minutes when conceding the opener under his leadership.

Sorensen, meanwhile, has won every match against RSL as the Caps boss, including their last two visits to America First Field, in which his team scored three goals both times.

Real Salt Lake Major League Soccer form:.

Vancouver Whitecaps Major League Soccer form:.

Due to a hamstring strain, Ariath Piol may miss this match for RSL, while Diego Luna and Emeka Eneli are questionable because of knee injuries and Zach Booth still has to clear concussion protocol.

Sergi Solans has scored three goals in his last two MLS home outings, including the opener in their 2-1 win over the Los Angeles Galaxy on Decision Day, while Rafael Cabral kept game one close, making six saves, many of them spectacular.

On the Vancouver side, an illness may keep Belal Halbouni out on Friday, and it is unlikely we will see Kenji Cabrera feature as he deals with a foot injury.

Edier Ocampo got the Caps on the board late in the opening half of game one, with Bruno Caicedo adding some insurance in the final 45 minutes.

Real Salt Lake possible starting lineup:.

Cabral; Yedlin, Glad, Quinton, Engel, Sanabria; Lobjanidze, Guske, Spierings, Guilavogui; Solans.

Vancouver Whitecaps possible starting lineup:.

Takaoka; Ocampo, Blackmon, Priso, Johnson; Larraz, Cubas; Sabbi, Muller, Caicedo; White.

The Caps have far too many weapons for RSL to contend with, and even a heroic Cabral between the sticks might not be enough to fend off the visitors given their current form.

By Matt Law | 25 Nov 2026 16:37, Last updated: 25 Nov 2026 16:40.

Manchester United are reportedly considering a move for Borussia Dortmund attacker Mathis Albert during next summer’s transfer window.

The 17-year-old joined Dortmund’s youth academy from LA Galaxy in 2024, and he has progressed to the first team at BVB, making four appearances.

Albert has only made three appearances for Dortmund this season, and it is understood that he is not presently happy with his playing time at the club.

According to Sky Deutschland, a switch during the January transfer window is not being ruled out, but a move to Old Trafford next summer is viewed as a possibility.

The report claims that newly introduced Man United head coach Mauricio Pochettino is a huge admirer of Albert and could push for his arrival in 2027.

Albert played under Pochettino for the USA, scoring once in five caps.

Pochettino’s arrival at Old Trafford has allegedly strengthened Man United’s chances of signing Albert, but the Red Devils are not the only club in the running for his signature.

Albert is primarily a left-sided attacker, but he is also capable of playing down the right or as a second striker.

The 5ft 10in forward had an excellent record for Dortmund’s Under-19s, scoring 14 goals and registering nine assists in 30 appearances.

Three of his four appearances for Dortmund have come in the Bundesliga, but he is yet to feature in the Champions League.

Man United are planning to be busy during the January transfer window, with the club at the moment struggling towards the bottom of the Premier League table.

A latest centre-back is high on Man United's wish-list, with Brentford's Nathan Collins and Fulham's Calvin Bassey both believed to be potential options at the start of 2027.

The 20-time English champions would also like to bring in a newly introduced centre-forward, but the club allegedly only have a £50m budget for the January window.

  • The attacking midfielder has registered four goal contributions in 11 games (across all competitions) this season.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Liverpool are reportedly showing ‘concrete interest’ in highly-rated Gladbach talent Wael Mohya.

The Bundesliga teenager is high up on the list at German giants Bayern Munich, with the Bavarians expected to face competition from Bayer Leverkusen for his signature.

The attacking midfielder has registered four goal contributions in 11 games (across all competitions) this season.

It has been revealed that christian Falk told CF Bayern Insider: “However, Bayern Munich definitely have him on the list. And we should note that both Liverpool and Brighton in the Premier League are showing concrete interest in the 17-year-old attacking talent.

“This is why Gladbach would be well-advised to try and offer him a new contract; that way, they can have some influence over how long the player stays at the club, or, at the very least, ensure that they get a sizeable sum from a permanent transfer.

It has been revealed that “I heard that there has already been contact with Mohya’s agent, Thies Bliemeister, and they talked about a move to Leverkusen. The next step is to talk to the player, his family and then the club. He doesn’t have a long-term contract at Gladbach, so there is a chance to make this deal happen.”.

With a contract right now set to expire in the summer of 2028, Mohya represents a genuine market opportunity for clubs looking to invest in a high-potential option.

On that note, Brighton makes a great deal of sense as the next stop in the 17-year-old’s career (if not his final destination), similarly to Leverkusen in the German top-flight.

Liverpool, it has to be said, would benefit greatly from a player with the Gladbach star’s profile, given they lack a viable backup option to Florian Wirtz in the ten position. Not to mention the fact that the footballer would provide further reassurance on the flanks.

Recent findings suggest that falk went on to add: “The 17-year-old was invited to the national team by Klopp during the international break. He wasn’t officially part of the squad; it was more just to give the player a taste of what international football looks like. He’s not totally clear yet about where he wants to commit, but Germany is putting up a strong fight to ensure that he pledges his international future to Die Nationalelf.”.

The big glitch facing Mohya in the coming weeks and months, of course, is whether a move to the likes of FC Bayern and Liverpool are actually in his best interest at this stage in his career.

Bayern Munich have Ismael Saibari and Jamal Musiala behind Harry Kane, albeit there are question marks over the latter’s long-term future in Munich in light of ongoing concerns over his health.

The Reds, of course, have Wirtz, in whom they invested a British transfer record fee (the total package being worth £116.5m). He’s played a significant percentage of the total minutes on offer in 2026/27 under upcoming boss Andoni Iraola, and at 23 years of age, he’s hardly at any risk of sinking past his peak in the near future.

We’ve no doubt Liverpool would welcome having a rotational option of Mohya’s quality, whom they could develop on their own time, and they can supply evidence of how well they’re managing Rio Ngumoha’s development despite the presence of more senior figures in Bradley Barcola and Cody Gakpo.

But if Wael Mohya’s looking for an absolute guarantee of regular minutes, you could forgive him for either staying put in Germany or joining the talent factory line in Brighton.
